entries.title: Tina Peters Is Back
entries.summary: Newly out of prison, she is back to trying to prove election fraud.
entries.content:
Earlier this year, Tina Peters was languishing in a Colorado women’s prison, eating processed food, and complaining of declining health—including a persistent cough, digestive issues, and bumps on her skin. But by the end of June, the woman who was convicted on charges tied to tampering with voting equipment under her control in 2020 strolled into the White House, sporting a tailored pinstripe suit and red lipstick, her hair cut in a sharp bob. She feasted on a fried-chicken-and-noodle dish with President Trump in his private dining room and posed for photos in the Oval Office. She told the president about her ordeal and “what prison does to a person,” and they both bemoaned the state of the nation’s voting systems. “He was kind. He listened,” Peters told me in an email.

Peters, once a martyr to the MAGA cause, is now a free woman, feted by the stolen-election movement. The former clerk and recorder of Mesa County, Colorado, was convicted in 2024 and sentenced to nearly nine years in prison after prosecutors said she deceived colleagues to grant an unauthorized person access to voting equipment. After returning to office, Trump, aided by his White House counsel and Justice Department, spearheaded a campaign to “Free Tina Peters” as MAGA commentators and her attorneys relentlessly used the power of their keyboards to demand her release. But because Peters was convicted of state charges, the only person with the power to get her out was Colorado Governor Jared Polis. The Democrat bowed to extraordinary pressure in May and granted Peters clemency despite pleas from prosecutors, his clemency board, and election officials that her punishment was just.

Peters was released on June 1 after serving about 20 months of her sentence. Her freedom came as Trump ordered the nation’s intelligence community to find proof of foreign interference in the 2020 presidential election—only for it to again come up empty. That hasn’t stopped Peters, who wants the government to go even further in its efforts to find fraud she alleges exists from 2020 and overhaul rules and systems over the next three months to prevent malfeasance in November’s midterm elections.

She walked out of prison repeating many of the unsubstantiated claims that helped land her behind bars. She immediately hit the MAGA circuit, appearing on podcasts and livestreams from locations that look straight out of Architectural Digest. She has crusaded against the machinery used to conduct American elections, insisting that votes have been flipped and that foreign adversaries could exploit future contests. She rails against prison conditions and calls for one of her critics—Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat—to be locked up. Her comeback tour has taken her around the country, including, on June 30, to the White House’s Presidential Walk of Fame, where a photo showed her glancing adoringly at Trump’s portrait while holding what appeared to be a Birkin bag. During the visit she and Trump talked about “election integrity,” Peters told me, including “why people need a process they can verify—paper, open counts, accountability.”

Peters has said in nearly all of these media appearances that the actions that landed her in prison were an attempt to expose irregularities in her county’s voting equipment. She insists that her incarceration was “retribution” for showing that votes could be flipped—though there is no evidence of that claim. Ahead of the midterms she is imploring Trump to declare a national emergency on elections as a way to try to assert federal control over contests that are, by constitutional design, run by state and local governments. “We don’t have to prove anymore that these machines are cheating, that the ballots are being harvested,” Peters told War Room, a show hosted by the Trump ally Steve Bannon. The chyron identified her as a Former Political Prisoner.

No longer subjected to rigid routines, head counts, or fixed mealtimes, Peters has enjoyed choosing her own food again, including steak, salads, and juicy tomatoes (“things that taste like they came from a kitchen instead of a tray.”) “Right now I’m trying to get healthy,” Peters told me. “See the people I love, and keep doing lawful work. I’m not interested in living bitter.” Her faith helped her endure especially tough moments. “I’m grateful to God,” she wrote. “Some days feel normal. Some don’t.” Peters must get permission from a parole officer before traveling out of state.

Election denial has become her full-time job. She directs supporters to her recently revamped website, where she asks that they contribute to her cause (a red “Donate” button hovers in the top-right corner). At a “Fraud Fighter Summit” off the Las Vegas Strip in June, Peters took the stage, clutching a bouquet of flowers, to the delight of the crowd, and a moderator gushed about how “wonderful” she looked. Peters talked on speakerphone with Roseanne Barr, who had planned to attend the conference but had to scrap her trip. “Congratulations for being released from detainment in a communist country, Tina,” the sitcom star said. “You are our hero.” They pledged to take a girls’ trip at some point soon. Hawaii, Peters said, sounded like a good destination, adding: “I can still travel.”

Peters has a history of finding herself embroiled in election disputes. She was elected Mesa County clerk and recorder in 2018 after campaigning on a promise to reopen a closed DMV office. Fruita, Colorado, got its motor-vehicles branch back, but Peters soon found herself in the middle of her first voting-related controversy. Nearly 600 ballots cast in a November 2019 election were found in a drop box outside the clerk’s office months later; an effort to recall Peters over the discovery failed to collect enough signatures. In November 2020 Trump won Mesa County, amassing nearly two-thirds of votes cast.

But that election, Peters claimed in 2021, was tainted. Prosecutors said that Peters ordered video cameras to be turned off and deceived colleagues to obtain credentials that allowed an election-denial activist to access election equipment. Peters ran for Colorado secretary of state, despite being charged with numerous felonies, on a platform that included the claim that election equipment posed a threat to democracy. She lost in the primary. In 2024, a jury found her guilty of seven charges, including four felonies. The judge presiding over the case called Peters a “charlatan” and said that Peters, not faulty equipment, posed a threat to the electoral process.

Trump returned to the Oval Office a few months after her conviction and quickly started a campaign to spring her from prison through pressure and threats of retaliation. He warned that “harsh measures” would ensue if she remained incarcerated and directed his Justice Department “to take all necessary action to help secure the release of this ‘hostage.’” Peters was convicted on state charges beyond Trump’s pardon power, but in December he issued one anyway. Senior U.S. District Court Judge R. Brooke Jackson, in a preliminary order blocking the administration’s threat to cut Colorado’s SNAP benefits, noted in March that Trump called Polis “weak and pathetic” for keeping Peters confined, and that the administration had launched “a barrage of threats and actions designed, by all appearances, to punish Colorado.” They included terminating millions of Department of Transportation funds, threatening cancellation of energy funds, announcing a plan to dismantle the Boulder-based National Center for Atmospheric Research, and denying federal disaster-relief assistance.

An appeals court upheld Peters’s conviction a few weeks later, but found that the judge who presided over her case may have improperly considered her public comments—violating her First Amendment rights—and ordered that she be resentenced. Instead, Polis decided to commute her sentence. He wrote that hers was an “extremely unusual and lengthy sentence for a first time offender who committed nonviolent crimes.” An addendum to her clemency application that I obtained shows she acknowledges having “made mistakes,” that she pledged to obey the law if released, and that she noted that she wouldn’t have the ability to commit similar crimes since she is no longer a county clerk. “My work to ensure honest elections,” she wrote, “will continue.”

When Peters was freed, on June 1, Francis McClelland was ready to greet her. Carrying a handmade sign reading Tina Peters Mahalo for Your Sacrifice Fight Fight Fight, the 69-year-old stood outside of the La Vista Correctional Facility in Pueblo with a handful of other supporters. McClelland had never understood why Peters would be imprisoned for trying to help prove that elections are rigged, and so he rented a car in Philadelphia and drove out to Colorado hoping to see her. But he made the trip in vain. Neither state-prison officials nor those close to her would say where she was, citing security concerns. “I just wanted to be in the area and if she saw the sign, just to know that, ‘Hey, man, you made a sacrifice,’” McClelland, an independent Trump supporter from Hawaii, told me. “You shouldn’t back down when you’re right,” he said. “I do believe she’s right.”

Peters told me her early days outside of prison were mostly quiet, and devoted to the simple pleasures of her new freedom. She slept, and ate avocados. She went outside without asking permission. “I called people,” she told me. “I hugged people. I did boring grown-up stuff you can’t do inside. It wasn’t a parade. It was me trying to feel like a person.”

In her first media appearance after her release, on War Room, Peters appeared alongside a friend and looked tired. “I feel like I’ve aged about 10 years,” she said. She called her release a “miracle” and thanked Trump, her attorneys, and the supporters who sent money through her website. She said she had a long road to clear her name and then went right back to the themes that had landed her in trouble, saying that Democrats “are going to cheat” in elections. “No one’s really addressing the problem that I spent my time in prison as retribution for,” she said. “And that was exposing the election machines that allow the votes to be flipped. As we’re coming up to our 250-year anniversary, I’m joyful that we still have our liberty but, at the same time, I’m very concerned and burdened with why no one is talking about this.”

The Tina Peters tour hasn’t stopped since. She joins the MAGA-sphere from a constantly changing rotation of tastefully decorated settings, including a room with small duck figurines in the background and another with furniture upholstered in black-and-white chevron. She was spotted at a gathering with Arizona’s Kari Lake, another prominent voice in the election-skeptic movement. And wherever she appears, she always implores viewers to hit that red “Donate” button on her site.

In June, a 12-hour online “Lift Tina Telethon” featured a roster of MAGA personalities applauding her sacrifice. She was likened to Joan of Arc and Nelson Mandela, and someone suggested that her face should be carved into Mount Rushmore. A banner crawling across the bottom of the screen asked viewers to Please DONATE NOW to reach a fundraising goal that one speaker set from $1 million to $2 million. Peters made her appearance midway through, and choked up almost immediately. She spoke of her time in prison, during which she wrote letters to Trump, and of a call she had with the president after her release. “I told him, ‘I only wrote two people while I was in prison,’” she said. “I got thousands and thousands of letters. I’m just so humbled and grateful because you guys were, and still are, the wind beneath my wings.” Peters said she told Trump she was discouraged that little progress had been made to secure election equipment. She hoped to talk more about it with him soon. She was staring down other problems, the kind that viewer donations might fix: Her air-conditioning had gone out, and so had the brakes on her truck. “It’s real difficult for me to ask for myself,” she said.

The tour’s biggest stop, the White House, came at Trump’s request, according to Peters’s attorney Peter Ticktin. “He really admires her because she’s an American hero—and he referred to her as such,” Ticktin, a longtime friend of the president’s, told me. “She’s the one he wanted to meet.” Ticktin declined to say what was discussed. Peters said she felt valued during that visit. She spoke with the president about what she saw as a county clerk, how prison affects people, and of the need for “paper, open counts, accountability” in elections. “He talked like he actually cares what happens to regular people,” she wrote to me, “which is not how a lot of papers write him up.” At one point during the visit, she clutched a red AMERICA IS BACK! hat. She also met with Ed Martin, the U.S. pardon attorney, and was presented with a gold eagle brooch representing the Eagle Forum, the conservative advocacy group founded by Phyllis Schlafly.

The White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson did not answer questions about the meeting with Peters, but said in a statement that “President Trump is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections, and that includes totally accurate and up-to-date voter rolls free of errors and unlawfully registered non-citizen voters.” Trump wants Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship and voter ID to vote, as well as “other legislative proposals that would establish a uniform standard of photo ID for voting, prohibit no-excuse mail-in voting, and end the practice of ballot harvesting,” Jackson wrote.

Two weeks after Peters visited the White House, Trump delivered a primetime address on election security, but again failed to provide clear evidence of fraud in the 2020 election. Many, including Peters, had hoped for more. On X, she called on Trump to “declare a National emergency” surrounding elections “to protect our country.” She later joined a handful of other election activists calling on federal officials to enforce a “Risk Mitigation Election Plan” before November that would, among other things, require hand-counting each ballot for federal contests before votes are certified, and compare them with counts tallied by electronic tabulators. “The objective is clear: reduce the opportunity for cheating,” read a July 24 letter from the activists to the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. CISA did not answer my questions about the activists’ proposed plan or a meeting the activists said they had with the agency.

Many of the people who administer America’s elections are dismayed by Peters’s post-prison celebrity. Her efforts to convince people that their elections can’t be trusted make the job of administrators more difficult and dangerous, they told me. “She didn’t learn a thing,” Carly Koppes, the Weld County, Colorado, clerk and recorder, said. “Her stance on ‘remorse’ is despicable, and she’s doing exactly what we told the governor she was going to do.” Tiffany Lee, the clerk and recorder from La Plata County, told me she and her staff cried with relief when Peters was sentenced. Now she is angry about what she termed Peters’s “sabotage” road show. "I knew for a fact that she would go right back to getting the attention," Lee said.

When I asked Peters what she would say to people who allege that her claims are false, she deflected. “I didn’t create the mistrust,” she wrote in the email. “For years the public got told everything was the most secure ever, and basic questions got treated like a threat. Now a lot of Americans say they don’t trust the process.”

Peters has her own ideas for making elections more secure. “Yelling at citizens won’t fix it. Proof will. Hand-marked paper. Paper poll books. Chain of custody. Counts people can watch, especially in federal races. That’s clearer than black-box machines and electronic poll books,” she wrote. “Making an election observable isn’t an attack on the country. It’s how you earn confidence back.” Election experts mostly dismiss these proposals as impractical, or warn they could produce large-scale errors.

Peters’s podcaster pals, attorneys, and online supporters told me they see her as a symbol of a broader resistance against forces of evil who are attempting to overtake America. “She’s very brave,” Steve Stern, a Republican activist in Broward County, Florida who hosts The Stern American Show on Rumble, told me. (Peters has treated his audience to interviews at least twice since her release.) “She’s trying to do something to help the country.”

Ticktin and another of her attorneys, John Case, told me they have earned no money from representing Peters. “Hopefully someday I’ll get fully compensated,” Case said, laughing. “But it’s doubtful. I’m not doing it for money—I’ll put it that way.” (At one point in his career, he charged $350 an hour.) Ticktin told me the work he’s doing at his own expense to help Peters is bigger than her: It’s about exposing “the biggest crime in the history of the United States—to steal our country.” Peters told me that some of her supporters were misled by fundraising pages that had nothing to do with her. Donations made on her website, she said, help pay for “legitimate costs: legal bills, security when needed,” and travel expenses for her advocacy work.

Her saga damaged some of her relationships with family members, she said. “That still stings,” she wrote. “I’m very grateful for my mom, for the family who stayed, and for the friends and supporters who didn’t throw me away.” She said she is doing ordinary things with family members and catching up on the past two years. When I talked briefly on the phone with her last month, she said she was traveling. “I’ll be in Texas tomorrow; I’ll be in different places the next few days,” she told me, her voice carrying a hint of a southern drawl. She later stressed that she’s traveling for work, not play.

When Peters first hit the election-activist circuit, the movement was dismissed by many elected officials and experts as “fringe.” Six years later, with Trump back in office and election deniers winning races up and down the ballot nationwide, the movement has been mainstreamed within the GOP even as the public’s trust in elections has declined. Their attempts to one day prove that 2020 was stolen may never bear fruit. But activists are already gearing up to uncover the fraud they believe might help Democrats win back Congress in 2026.

entries.title: What True Crime Gets Wrong About Crime
entries.summary: The hit Netflix documentary Maternal Instinct tidies a far more complicated story.
entries.content:
The hit Netflix documentary Maternal Instinct tidies a far more complicated story.

On October 9, 2020, Taylor Parker, a 27-year-old mother of two, visited her friend Reagan Simmons-Hancock at her home in northeastern Texas. Simmons-Hancock, who was 35 weeks pregnant with her second child, had something Parker felt she desperately needed: a baby.

What transpired next is the subject of Maternal Instinct, a hit Netflix true-crime documentary directed by Jessica Dimmock and released in June. If you watched the film, you might conclude that you know everything you need to know about Parker and her crimes. But you would be mistaken. What is remarkable—albeit in line with the demands of the true-crime genre—is just how much Maternal Instinct leaves out.

True-crime documentaries are entertainment. They tend to follow a formula with common elements: villains and victims, mystery and suspense, capture and catharsis. These stories typically adopt the tropes of horror films—eerie music, ominous foreshadowing—and offer the prosecution’s version of events, which favor a tidy and dramatic view of a killer’s means and motives. The defense’s job is to poke holes in these assumptions. By omitting vital details from defense teams—in Parker’s case and others—true-crime films portray the grisliest offenses as essentially incomprehensible expressions of wickedness, when the reality is invariably more complicated.

The documentary opens with an acquaintance of Parker’s observing that “there’s evil in our land” and that “evil people do evil things.” This is more of a spiritual explanation than a legal or clinical one. No one can know the fundamental character of another person’s soul, but Maternal Instinct hardly tries to understand Parker’s. Parker is clearly guilty of committing two horrifying murders. Her evident mental illness does, however, challenge the claim that her actions could be explained only by inveterate evil.

As Maternal Instinct recounts, in the months prior to that October morning in Simmons-Hancock’s home, Parker, a divorced mother of two, had staged a fake pregnancy. She had gone to great lengths to convince the people around her—including her fairly new boyfriend—that she was expecting. She’d padded her belly, fabricated medical documents and ultrasounds, and claimed that coronavirus-pandemic restrictions mandated that she see her doctors solo. But unbeknownst to her boyfriend and others, Parker was infertile, having undergone a hysterectomy years earlier.

To keep her lies from being exposed, Parker sought a newborn child to make her own. According to police, she arrived at the house of her very pregnant friend with a scalpel and bludgeoned the 21-year-old Simmons-Hancock with what was likely a hammer, then wrestled her to the floor, sliced her uterus open, and extracted her unborn child. Parker then fled the scene with the infant, leaving Simmons-Hancock to die; the infant died later that day. In 2022, after two years in prison and a weekslong trial, Parker was found guilty of capital murder by a Texas jury and sentenced to death.

Maternal Instinct is meant to paint a portrait of a criminal and her crime, but Parker, who remains on death row, was neither interviewed nor consulted for the documentary—nor were her defense attorneys or their expert witnesses, though Dimmock and her team offered them a chance to comment before releasing the film. Dimmock explained to me that she’d declined to interview Parker out of respect for Simmons-Hancock’s family and friends, and because she doubted that Parker would be truthful or remorseful.

True-crime stories about female killers tend to be especially titillating. Men are about nine times more likely to commit murder than women—who are assumed to be, as the Cornell Law School professor Sandra Babcock put it, “peaceful, nurturing, mothering, caring, obedient.” Murder “seems so out of step with how we view women, how we perceive the stereotypical woman as being,” Babcock, who specializes in gender rights and the death penalty, told me.

Parker’s trial gave rise to a profusion of lurid headlines: “Texas Woman Allegedly Stabbed Mom-to-Be 100 Times, Then Tried to Steal Baby from Womb,” reported People magazine; “Neurologist: Taylor Parker’s Brain Is ‘Broken;’ Defense Rests,” offered the local NBC affiliate KTAL News. Body-cam clips of Parker’s interactions with police spread on YouTube and TikTok. The coverage inspired Maternal Instinct and sets its tone; Dimmock told me that much of her team’s preliminary research into Parker’s case came from the news articles and video clips disseminated online.

Maternal Instinct includes interviews with Parker’s former friends and acquaintances, who describe the broad scope of Parker’s lies over the years, including her many allegedly fictitious ailments and her claims that she was due to receive a multimillion-dollar inheritance from her oil-baron grandparents, who were, in reality, of no particular means. To maintain her deceptions about the pregnancy and other matters, Parker owned multiple cellphones for sending fraudulent messages, fabricated official letters, and used voice-altering software to place anonymous calls.

Randi Chavez, an investigator brought on by Parker’s attorneys, met with Parker for hundreds of hours over the course of a year. Chavez retained experts to assess Parker’s mental and neurological health, and she interviewed people who knew her, including relatives and fellow prisoners. What she discovered was that Parker had displayed symptoms of profound mental illness for many years.

To stipulate that Parker’s mental illness played a significant role in her ghastly crimes is not to suggest that she should have been found either incompetent to stand trial or not guilty by reason of insanity, both of which are exceedingly rare outcomes. Her defense instead presented evidence of her mental illness as a factor that ought to have spared her from the death penalty, but not from punishment altogether. (The American Psychiatric Association, the American Bar Association, and other professional groups have called for a ban on the death penal­ty for those with severe mental illness.) Yet like Parker’s jury, Maternal Instinct does not take Parker to be seriously mentally ill.

At Parker’s trial, the prosecution called upon the forensic psychiatrist Michael Arambula to testify that Parker showed signs of borderline personality disorder, a condition marked by intense mood swings, unstable relationships, impulsivity, fear of abandonment, and feelings of emptiness. But Arambula’s testimony undermined the seriousness of the illness by likening it to intentionally malicious behavior. Borderline personality disorder, he told the jury, is “probably the most manipulative of the personality types.” Parker, he said, had a “pleasant and engaging demeanor atop a core of rage.” He denied that mental illness had contributed to Parker’s murders, insisting to the jury that the uncommon brutality of her crimes did not mean that she was delusional. Members of Simmons-Hancock’s family have likewise adamantly maintained that Parker is “evil” rather than “crazy.”

But Arambula delivered his testimony without ever meeting or interviewing Parker. He drew his conclusions from a review of Parker’s medical records. The defense’s mental-health experts, who’d actually met Parker, came to very different conclusions.

At trial, the defense called a psychiatrist, a neurologist, and a social worker, all of whom confirmed that Parker suffered from a personality disorder that was exacerbated by a personal history of trauma and abuse. They found that Parker’s teenage mother had been negligent, disengaged, and hostile to her daughter before abandoning the family when Parker was a teenager. Her father, meanwhile, had abused methamphetamines, and when Parker was 12, he’d taken her to a house frequented by drug users, where, she said, a man raped her. Maternal Instinct neither reported nor probed those allegations.

After Parker’s conviction, lawyers working on her appeals invited more experts to expand this evidence. Nicole Anders, a clinical psychologist for the defense who met with Parker in January 2025, confirmed that Parker displayed traits associated with borderline personality disorder and argued that this condition—which Anders discussed in the context of Parker’s history of trauma and abuse—significantly altered her ability to reason or function. In a declaration submitted to the court, Anders stated that the trauma and sexual abuse Parker endured as a child had left her hypervigilant, prone to delusion, and desperate for emotional connection. “Although these coping strategies may be maladaptive in the long term,” Anders wrote in her clinical report, “they are rooted in survival instincts. When safe, consistent caregiving is absent or unpredictable early in life, the nervous system adapts to prioritize protection over connection or reason.”

Craig Malkin, a lecturer in psychology at Harvard Medical School, told me that personality disorders form when a patient’s ways of coping with traumatic experiences become deeply ingrained. “We all develop some kind of psychological armor,” Malkin said, which “are just ways of protecting ourselves in vulnerable moments when we’re ashamed, when we fear rejection, when we’re sad and helpless.” For Parker, coping with her mother’s rejection, her father’s destructive irresponsibility, and her own desolate loneliness meant developing delusional fantasies and resorting to extreme people-pleasing behavior. Winning the affection of others sometimes meant lying to them about what she had to offer. Borderline patients, Malkin said, “are people who live on the edge of neurosis and psychosis,” meaning that they alternate between struggling to solve everyday problems and losing touch with reality altogether.

According to experts who spoke with Parker during and after her trial, those delusions centered on her fertility. In 2014, six years before the murders, Parker sought a routine tubal ligation to prevent further pregnancies, but the procedure failed. When a gynecologist confirmed to Parker a year later that she was pregnant, Parker was relieved. She concluded that it was a sign from God that she was meant to have another child. But during a subsequent surgery to remove a cyst on her right ovary, her doctor discovered that the pregnancy was ectopic and developing in her left fallopian tube. While Parker was still under anesthesia, her surgical team procured consent from her then-husband to undertake a total abdominal hysterectomy, removing Parker’s fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and right ovary. Although Maternal Instinct notes that Parker’s hysterectomy left her unable to have children, the film neglects to mention how it happened or how she felt about it.

Parker was shattered when she awoke to find that she could no longer bear children. She confided in friends at the time and later told Diana Barnes, a women’s-mental-health expert brought in by her defense team, that she felt robbed of her identity and purpose in life. She became fixated on pregnancy and childbirth, took a job at a women’s health clinic to be near babies, spent her free time watching mothers and children at parks and stores, and desperately researched surrogacy and uterine transplants, even soliciting her mother for her uterus. As Parker’s obsession progressed, her marriage broke down, and her mental health unraveled. She told others that she had again become pregnant and miscarried, though that was not possible. She told Barnes that when she placed a mock pregnancy belly on her body in 2020, she felt as though it were really her flesh.

Parker was clearly unwell in the months and years leading up to the murders, a fact that Maternal Instinct elides. The documentary suggests that Parker’s crimes were carefully calculated out of selfishness and deceit: A malevolent young woman conspired to entrap her boyfriend with a fake pregnancy and needed a newborn to pull off the plot, so she brutally murdered a friend and stole her baby. But that version of events raises questions that can be answered only by Parker’s mental illness: Why was her desire for love and acceptance so overwhelming that it curdled into criminality? What made the prospect of having a baby with her boyfriend seem worth killing for? Suggesting that Parker’s evil nature alone explains her many schemes and lies is both reductive and unsatisfying.

The film does not explain how someone so adept at weaving elaborate falsehoods might fail to anticipate that staff at the hospital where she arrived with Simmons-Hancock’s baby would also inquire into her own condition. People who had doubted her pregnancy were bound to notice that Simmons-Hancock’s murder and Parker’s “birth” had coincided. But Parker was not thinking clearly, and had not been for some time.

Murder is, after all, not a good idea. Some people commit murder without having thought it through at all, but that sort of crime does not make one eligible for the death penalty. Murders that are eligible for the death penalty involve some degree of premeditation and intent. The presence of planning is usually taken to be proof that a murderer had a sober appreciation for what they meant to do, but it also suggests that something was seriously wrong with their capacity to reason; otherwise, they would have come to the conclusion that, whatever their predicament, murder could only compound it. This does not seem to have occurred to Taylor Parker.

The origins of many murders eligible for the death penalty seem to lie less in deeply rooted inherent wickedness than in particularly compromised minds. Such nuance is usually absent from true-crime yarns, however, because acknowledging mental illness and other impairments complicates simplistic narratives. The genre captivates audiences by dramatizing the worst human behavior, but these stories almost always neglect to illuminate the whole truth, which is stranger and more tragic than what passes for good TV.

entries.title: Why I Love Blue Books
entries.summary: There’s no better way for students to show their professors what they’re capable of.
entries.content:
The humble booklet is more than just a last redoubt against cheating. Staring down its empty pages, students discover what they’re capable of as writers and thinkers.

Across the faded blue covers of the exam books in my attic, I can trace the arc of my academic career. I can still see the grades I received on tests in “The Meaning of Abstraction in Modern Art” (A) and in Neurobiology (B–). Just the sight of the booklets is enough for me to feel the pressure to perform, to sculpt the contents of a semester’s worth of knowledge into some fresh shape. But by the time I became a college professor myself, in 2013, the blue book had begun to disappear. Why struggle to discern student penmanship, or risk misplacing a final exam in the trunk of one’s Subaru (to cite a completely hypothetical example), when tests, like everything else, can be administered on a laptop?

The coronavirus made every aspect of education virtual, but even after it abated, in-person final exams remained out of favor for many classes. Part of the reason was simply administrative—the challenge of finding faculty or graduate students to watch over the test-takers. But there was also a shift in how teachers appraised student learning. The blue book meant timed essays and handwritten work, modes of assessment that felt regressive, cruel. It recalled an age of higher education—punitive and bleak, the domain of Dickens’s stern Mr. Gradgrind—that the modern university was eager to outgrow. Not entirely, of course; some faculty still lugged boxes of blue books home in the snow and scribbled grades in red on the covers. But alternatives to the in-person exam proliferated: the capstone project, the take-home essay, the portfolio of selected work from the semester.

The blue book seemed destined to become a relic, as obsolete as cursive. But it had one virtue that hasn’t been easy to replicate: Cheating on a blue-book exam is difficult. When faculty moved away from in-person pen-and-paper exams, they assumed that cheating would be kept in check by honor codes, or by “locked” browsers, which would prevent students from accessing sites that would jog their memory or simply give them the answers. But these measures were never wholly effective. In a survey of undergraduates published in 2020, 62 percent admitted to cheating in some manner.

The advent of AI has only exacerbated the problem. In a matter of seconds, students can create an entire essay with the help of a chatbot. If they’re savvy, they can spend a bit more time to make it sound authentically human enough to evade detection by their professor. As my colleague Rose Horowitch has reported, such cheating has become so prevalent that Princeton recently gave up on its venerable honor code. For 133 years, students had signed a pledge not to cheat, and professors had trusted them to do the right thing. In May, in the face of rampant AI-enabled cheating, the university’s faculty voted to begin proctoring exams for the first time since the Gilded Age.

Universities find themselves in a surprising position. The only reliable way to evaluate what students have learned may be to bring back pen and paper. Faculty are reverting to in-person, handwritten assignments and timed essays—anything that keeps assessments offline. The unlikely hero of the day is the blue book, sales of which are up by as much as 80 percent for some universities since 2023.

Yet the blue book is more than a last redoubt against cheating. Despite its antiquated appearance, the blue book encourages experimentation, even virtuosity. It deserves to live on not because of what it rejects but because of what it makes possible: thinking on the page, a hallmark of the humanities that is indispensable to their value—and essential to the kinds of human beings that a liberal-arts institution hopes to send out into the world.

The blue book hasn’t changed much for a hundred years or more, with its sky-blue tint and pale-red margin lines, its two neat staples and wide-open spacing, and its austere list of requirements on the cover (NAME, SUBJECT, CLASS, SECTION). The precise history of the blue book is lost to time. One origin story pinpoints its emergence in the 1920s at Butler University; the pamphlet is said to have borrowed its distinctive hue from the university’s colors. Harvard lore suggests that the blue book is older still: By one account, a classics instructor, Evangelinus Apostolides Sophocles, burned a stack of blue-book exams to protest the university’s move from oral to written examinations in 1857.

I realize that by advocating for the blue book in 2026, I might be engaging in the same opposition to progress as old Professor Sophocles. But to me, the blue book represents a timeless human activity—namely, trusting your mind to discover unknown capabilities.

I think of my college-age self, looking up at the clock as I turned the page, crossed out a sentence, broke the tip of my pencil. I recall the satisfaction of filling one book and getting up from my desk to take another, the adrenaline of using my knowledge to improvise something and then having more to say. What I learned by writing this way was distinct from what I learned by composing a five-paragraph essay, with its thesis statement, staid structure, and rote deployment of argument and evidence. Any AI agent can mimic that template.

Taking a blue-book exam is an almost athletic endeavor, and not just because of the stamina it requires of both mind and hand. The test-taker is forced to compose an essay that will demonstrate their command of a semester’s or year’s worth of material. They have to summon the verve to tackle a prompt about the place of freedom in the American novel, or the value of a human life in Hamlet, or what Whitman meant when he said that “the United States themselves are essentially the greatest poem.” Staring down the empty pages of a blue book, I learned to throw myself into my writing. In the process, I discovered what I was capable of as a writer and a thinker. When you’ve done the reading and reviewed your lecture notes, you can feel like a basketball player whose hours in the gym made possible a transcendent playoff performance, or like a musician whose endless runs of arpeggios in a soundproof practice room allowed for a spectacular solo in the concert hall.

Not every student can put pencil to paper for 90 minutes without looking up. Even the strongest students can struggle, at first, to answer the question, or to organize their thoughts. But this, too, is a reason to love the blue book. When students write, they write into uncertainty. They court risk. No surrogate exists for feeling an idea form in your mind and trying to express that idea on the page. And wonderfully, for the instructor, the blue book documents how students strain their way to an answer or an argument. The marks on the page are indelible, and efforts to amend them leave marks of their own: furious erasing or hasty strike-throughs. The blue book is a record of first thoughts, instincts, intuitions.

These fits and starts and failed experiments are a good thing—for the education of the individual and for the health of a society. The humanities are distinguished by the habits of mind that they inculcate, not for their success in forcing students to memorize facts. Among the most significant of these habits are a nimbleness of thought and a flexibility of argument, the ability to draw connections between diverse sets of facts. Those habits are honed by writing under pressure. Challenged by the blue book, students learn to identify and stand behind their individual commitments. As their professor, I hope they carry that lesson beyond the classroom, beyond the university, and into the fractious world they enter as citizens.

Often the key insight arrives just as time is expiring, and I love how no part of the book is out of bounds for a final thought at the buzzer. “Education is the single greatest thing Thoreau believes in,” one student sneaks into the margins of the final for my American-literature course. For the teacher, this is the pleasure of the blue book—despite its uniform presentation and its rigid lineation, any part of it might reveal a sudden moonshot of an idea. Many of the best sentences appear on the back inside cover, such as this ending to an essay on Toni Morrison: “A good life is what we make it to be—now all we have to do is live it.”

Students, of course, know what they’ve been taught: the timeline of the English Civil War, the structure of a sonnet by Gwendolyn Brooks, the development of a motif in a Mahler symphony. But the blue book demands more than a recitation of facts. It asks students to demonstrate not just that they know when or where something happened, but why it did. It asks them not just who wrote a poem, or when, but what the poem conveys about the world in which it was written. The best-prepared students, the ones who inhabit the history and poetry and music that have made up the semester’s syllabus, find that they understand the material in ways they didn’t appreciate before they opened the blue book and the clock started ticking.

Proponents of artificial intelligence have promised that, by removing certain elements of the craft of writing, students can concentrate on making their work more polished and their ideas more clearly defined. That’s a dangerous ruse. To see what a student has learned, look at the moment when they struggle to begin—and then transcend that struggle to create something genuinely surprising. That’s the moment the full force of the writer’s mind takes possession of the process.

When we eliminate the possibility of writing badly or incoherently, we eliminate writing’s greatest satisfaction: the feeling that we have stepped outside ourselves and are watching our own words fall together in the right order. What I describe sounds like a state of grace, but it’s also a furious act of intellection and expression undertaken with only one’s study and wits to guide them. I’ve come to love handing out blue books on exam day and seeing the look of ready intelligence on my students’ faces. The essay they are about to write will be better than they think it can be. All they have to do is write it.

This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “The Blue Book Is Back.”

entries.title: Iran Goes Looking for Love in Jordan
entries.summary: Tehran wants the Arab public to balk at the cost of allying with the United States.
entries.content:
Tehran wants the Arab public to balk at the cost of allying with the United States.

In late July, Iran struck a U.S. military base in Jordan, killing three American service members. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps followed up with an unusual series of messages to the Jordanian people: “You know well that we have no hostility toward your country,” the IRGC declared in a statement published on Iran’s Fars News Agency. “Rather, we love you, noble people who understand the suffering and injustice endured by the Palestinian people more than any other nation.”

Another message cheekily thanked unnamed Jordanians for providing targeting information for the Iranian strikes. A third appeared to address Jordanian critics of the operation, saying that the United States, not Iran, had “violated your territorial integrity and sovereignty.”

The appeals to Jordanians speak to a concerted effort, fueled by Iran’s growing confidence in its regional position since the start of the war with the United States and Israel, to convince the Arab public that an alliance with the United States is not worth the cost. The Islamic Republic has tried to drive such a wedge ever since its founding in 1979. But today’s push reflects Tehran’s perception of what Iranian officials call a “new equation of power” in the Middle East—one that includes Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has demonstrated its willingness to defend this position through missile strikes on seven different Arab countries that host U.S. bases. At least three were aimed at Jordan, including a surprise attack on July 28. Now the IRGC is reaching out to Jordanians with professions of solidarity and love.

The switch from bombardment to flattery may seem sudden, and Jordan may seem an unlikely place for the IRGC to go looking for friends. Unlike Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, Jordan has no significant Shiite minority to form a social base for the spread of Iranian influence. But Tehran has both a military rationale and an ideological one.

Iran’s military purpose is clear: Jordan houses radar and anti-missile systems that help Israel detect and deter incoming Iranian fire, and it lacks the military capacity to retaliate against Iranian strikes. Jordan also lacks the economic clout that seems to have helped the United Arab Emirates—an essential export hub for Iranian goods—cut a tacit nonaggression pact with Tehran, at least for the moment.

Tehran also hopes to exploit a fissure between Jordan’s people and their government, which depends on the protection and patronage of the United States. Some Jordanians have recently called for the expulsion of the U.S. military, a movement fueled in part by deep sympathy for the Palestinian cause. Some 60 percent of Jordan’s population is of Palestinian origin.

Ever since the start of the Gaza war in 2023, street protests have regularly erupted in Jordan. These have been supported by the country’s king and queen and by prominent government officials, whether out of conviction or a belief that the public needs to let off steam. Queen Rania gave an interview to Christiane Amanpour two weeks after the Hamas massacre on October 7 in which she spoke of Israeli actions as a “genocide”—a gesture that was widely seen in Jordan (and Israel) as setting a new tone of fury regarding Israel’s behavior in Gaza.

Jordanian demonstrators did more than let off steam: They pledged support for Hamas. Islamist networks in Jordan began gaining strength, leading the government to ban the local chapter of the Muslim Brotherhood last year. In late 2024, Jordanians, two of whom were members of the Brotherhood, carried out two cross-border terrorist attacks in Israel.

Violence in Gaza has ebbed since a cease-fire took hold late last year, but Israel’s gradual, de facto annexation of the West Bank, which has accelerated in the past few years under Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government, is of deep concern to Jordan. The specter of a fuller or even formal annexation—however unlikely at the moment—raises profound fears in Jordan of a flood of Palestinian refugees, which might upset the country’s fragile demographic balance and amplify anger at Israel.

“The Iranians believe they know what’s going on in Jordan,” Amer al-Sabaileh, a Jordanian security expert and columnist, told me. “This could be a multilayered strategy—missiles, then propaganda, then maybe activating cells.”

But Iran’s bets may well prove wrong. For all their sympathy with the Palestinian cause, Jordanians have long been profoundly distrustful of Iran’s revolutionary Shiite project, partly for sectarian reasons, given that Jordan’s people are almost all Sunni Muslims. Tehran’s latest missile blitz aimed at its neighbors is also taking a toll. Recent polling in Arab countries suggests that any sympathy Iran gained during the initial phase of the war this spring, when it was seen as a victim of Israeli aggression, evaporated with Tehran’s recent bout of air strikes on Arab countries, says Michael Robbins, the director of the Arab Barometer, a public-opinion-research organization.

Jordanian officials, who spoke obliquely of defending Jordanian sovereignty during the first phase of the Israeli-U.S. war earlier this year, have taken a firm line against “Iranian aggression” in recent public statements. So have some of the country’s government-aligned journalists.

“Jordan is subjected to Iranian aggression, full stop,” wrote the columnist Hussein al-Rawasdeh, in an article in the newspaper al-Dustour that criticized those calling for the withdrawal of U.S. troops as disloyal. “Do you stand with your country?” Other columnists went further, suggesting that the Iranian strikes might even stiffen Arab resolve and help form a more united front.

But Arab countries confront limited options. “Ultimately, they all face the same strategic calculation that adopting a harder line against Iran, especially as ultra-hard-liners gain influence in Tehran, will place them more firmly in the crosshairs,” Ahmad Sharawi, a senior analyst at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, told me. Their primary weapon, he said, will remain “diplomatic condemnations.”

entries.title: Ukraine’s Fleeting Turnaround
entries.summary: The chorus of optimism has quieted on several fronts, including Zelensky’s struggle with corruption and his relations with Trump.
entries.content:
The chorus of optimism has quieted on several fronts, including Zelensky’s struggle with corruption and his relations with Trump.

Earlier this summer, Ukraine had finally seized the initiative in its punishing four-year war. President Volodymyr Zelensky had plenty of dramatic victories and technological advances to tout to his Western backers as he made the case that Russia can be defeated. His clash with Donald Trump in the Oval Office last year had been eclipsed by more recent encounters in which the U.S. president seemed open to helping Ukraine prevail. After closed-door talks with Zelensky in Turkey last month, Trump offered to meet Kyiv’s desperate need for air defenses and told reporters during a briefing about the two leaders’ promising vibe: “There was a lot of love in that room, a lot of unity.”

In Washington, Zelensky also had a well-connected ambassador in place. Olha Stefanishyna, a former deputy prime minister, was constantly describing Ukraine’s battlefield successes to officials and lawmakers. Her goal was to move beyond those sympathetic to Kyiv’s plight to build “reliable, economic, interest-based relations across America,” she told us in an interview.

That momentum, built up since the start of the year, fizzled in a matter of days. At his meeting with Zelensky last week, Trump did not agree to send more of the Patriot air-defense systems that Ukraine needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles. He also backtracked on his pledge to let Ukrainian companies make these systems themselves. Back in Kyiv, long-festering issues related to wartime corruption weakened Zelensky’s team, leading to the ouster of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last month and the resignation of Stefanishyna earlier this week. (She returned to Kyiv to address corruption allegations, which she denies.)

In a rare show of public dissent, protesters have rallied for weeks in Kyiv to demand that Zelensky reinstate the defense minister. His reengagement may be vital to Zelensky’s plan for Ukraine to survive the winter. Zelensky had asked Trump during their meeting to call in a favor from Elon Musk, The Atlantic first reported last week; Musk’s SpaceX operates the Starlink satellite system. Zelensky wants to use the system to guide strikes against the missile batteries that Russia uses to hammer Kyiv and other cities. Trump was noncommittal about that proposal too. Since he was dismissed, Fedorov has been working through back channels to appeal to Musk, who so far has refused to relent, two of Fedorov’s close allies in Kyiv told us.

“As of this moment, there is no positive decision,” one of those allies said on Wednesday. Musk continues to argue with Fedorov over the risk of further Russian escalation in the war. “Elon keeps saying it’s time to make a deal,” the Fedorov ally said. (Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.)

After the Oval Office meeting with Zelensky, Trump said that his trusted envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would make their first visit to wartime Kyiv in the coming days. But there are no other signs indicating that the pair will make the trip, despite Witkoff’s eight visits to Moscow as Trump’s envoy. Ukrainian officials are skeptical that the real-estate tycoons, who would have to make the long train ride to Kyiv from Poland, will show up anytime soon.

All of these developments have been as unwelcome as they are painfully familiar for Ukraine’s leadership: Throughout the war, they have seen the resolve of their most important ally falter in the moments when it has mattered most—and when a real breakthrough seemed within reach. The White House, fearful of Kremlin retaliation and worried about a shortage of munitions during its war with Iran, has left Kyiv to face another winter of Russian bombardment, just weeks after things finally appeared to be looking up.

A senior administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity to address internal deliberations, told us that the United States was exploring options for defense-industry cooperation with Ukraine but suggested, as Trump has publicly in recent weeks, that following through with his promise to grant Ukraine the ability to manufacture Patriot systems could endanger America’s military edge. “We must prioritize protecting these exquisite systems and expanding overall production of critical weapons systems for the U.S. warfighter and for our partners and allies,” the official said in a statement.

At a meeting of his war council on Wednesday, Zelensky mused that his foreign partners might have darker motives for withholding the air defenses that his country needs. “Maybe these are political steps aimed at making Ukraine more, let’s call it, compliant,” he said in televised remarks. “In my view, that’s also part of it.”

Perhaps the Ukrainians should have seen this coming. After Trump won the election in 2024, many of Zelensky’s allies in Kyiv clung to naive expectations for his second term. They had grown deeply frustrated with what they viewed as the Biden administration’s lack of urgency in providing Ukraine with high-powered weapons. A common refrain in Kyiv held that Joe Biden, due to his fear of escalation, gave them enough to survive the war but not enough to win.

Officials in Kyiv had hoped that Trump might jump-start negotiations with the Kremlin after he repeatedly promised to end the war quickly. “We needed to show that we were not the obstacle to peace,” a senior Ukrainian official told us about that period. “The obstacle is Russia, and we need to overcome it together.”

This became the central message of Ukrainian diplomacy during the U.S. presidential transition, and Zelensky delivered it to Trump at every opportunity. But Trump wanted to see some tangible benefit for the United States in supporting Ukraine. Senator Lindsey Graham, a confidant of both Trump and Zelensky, came up with a plan for the U.S. to profit from its role in the war through the extraction of Ukraine’s natural resources, especially rare earth minerals. Zelensky balked at the plan’s most onerous provisions, which seemed to turn Ukraine from an American ally into an economic vassal. He rejected drafts presented to him by J. D. Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, among others.

Stefanishyna, then serving as both the deputy prime minister and the justice minister, helped design a compromise that both sides could accept. She hoped the signing ceremony at the White House, which she attended, would be a brief, cordial affair. The now-famous encounter last February instead devolved into a televised fracas, in which Trump and Vance accused Zelensky of ingratitude and disrespect. Trump’s aides asked the Ukrainian delegation to leave the White House. “Complete and utter disaster,” Graham fumed to reporters gathered outside the West Wing.

Looking back, Stefanishyna told us, Zelensky and his aides hadn’t come prepared to make Ukraine’s case in a way that would resonate with Trump. They didn’t realize the extent to which Trump and his aides viewed Ukraine’s suffering—at least 16,000 civilian deaths have been documented, in addition to nearly half a million soldiers killed or wounded—as a Democratic cause. Biden had spearheaded the Western coalition in support of Ukraine and sought to make his defense of Ukraine’s sovereignty a defining issue of his presidency. With Trump back in power, this all worked in Russia’s favor. “We came with all this pain to the White House,” she said, “and it became very obvious that this was our pain” and not something shared by the Trump administration. Although Trump may have empathized on some level, she added, “as president of the United States, he has a very different perspective. This was a wake-up.”

The administration official said that Trump and his team remain committed to contributing to the war’s end. “We are the only country in the world that can play that role,” the official said.

In July of last year, Stefanishyna arrived in the U.S. to represent Ukraine in Washington. Soon after, Trump hosted Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska. Stefanishyna was horrified to see the Russian president get a much warmer reception than Zelensky had in February. The summit ended Putin’s long global isolation without Trump demanding a single concession. The moment generated a “very physical fear,” Stefanishyna said. “To wake up in the morning in a reality where the United States is coming back to friendly relations with Russia,” she said, was “like Ukraine never existed.” The rapprochement “was much more terrifying than living in Ukraine under bombs.”

Through the bitterly cold winter that followed, in which temperatures fell below zero Fahrenheit, Russian missiles hammered Ukraine’s power grid and heating infrastructure, leaving millions of civilians to freeze in darkened homes or bomb shelters. Many saw this as the low point for Kyiv in the war.

Ukraine survived. But by the middle of winter, Russia had figured out a potent new way to attack. Russian troops were guiding their drones in Ukraine with the help of Starlink. “This could have been a real catastrophe,” Fedorov told us. The technology allowed the Russians to circumvent Ukraine’s air defenses and bombard any target they wanted, including the government district in Kyiv. To stop them, Fedorov reached out to Musk with an urgent appeal for help.

The billionaire called him back at the end of January, when Fedorov happened to be at his daughter’s birthday party, and the minister stepped out to chat with Musk, whose face appeared on the screen of his phone. That conversation led to a plan to cut off Russian access to Starlink terminals. Ukrainian forces continued to fly their drones with Starlink inside Ukrainian territory, including in Crimea and other Russian-occupied regions.

The technological imbalance allowed Ukraine to shift the momentum at the front, where its troops reclaimed a few hundred square kilometers of occupied territory by the middle of February. Around the same time, Ukraine began a campaign of long-range strikes targeting Russian oil refineries. It also used drones early this summer to cut off Russian supply lines to Crimea. Moscow and other cities soon faced fuel shortages, and Kremlin-backed authorities in Crimea declared a state of emergency. For the first time in years, Ukraine appeared to have Russia on the back foot.

The White House noticed. “The real factor that has changed the U.S. attitude, including President Trump, is success on the battlefield by the Ukrainians,” William Taylor, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, told us regarding its recent battlefield gains. He noted Russia’s staggering casualty rate, far higher than Ukraine’s. After all, Taylor added: “Trump likes to back a winner.”

The start of the war in Iran at the end of February—as it happens, one year to the day after Zelensky’s clash with Trump in the Oval Office—gave Stefanishyna another chance to make Ukraine’s case around Washington. Ukraine had invented a way to shoot down the cheap drones that Iran was using to target Persian Gulf nations and U.S. bases in the Middle East. The Ukrainian interceptor drones cost as little as $1,000 to produce, compared with millions for sophisticated U.S. interceptor missiles. “We discovered that we are the only country on the whole planet who’s able to provide effective means of defense in that regard,” Stefanishyna told us. The innovation gave Ukraine the opportunity to engage with the United States not as a supplicant asking for aid but as a partner.

Zelensky offered to share the technology with the U.S. and its allies in the Middle East. Trump did not seem interested. “We don’t need their help in drone defense,” he told Fox News in March, days after a deadly drone attack on the U.S. base in Kuwait. “We know more about drones than anybody.”

Others in his administration saw it differently. In congressional testimony in May, U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said that he had learned a lot from the Ukrainians. Their military operating system, known as Delta, “is absolutely incredible,” Driscoll said. “It fully integrates every single drone, every sensor, and every shooting platform into just one single network. Ours does not.”

Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure also bolstered the impression of momentum shifting in Ukraine’s favor. “Now everybody in Washington thinks Ukraine is going to win,” one Republican strategist told us last week. “They have all these drones, and we want all these drones.”

Following what Trump called a “very good meeting” with Zelensky on the sidelines of a G7 summit in June, the U.S. president piled pressure on Putin, saying that “Russia should make a deal.” Then came Trump and Zelensky’s talks at the NATO conference in Ankara, Turkey, last month, where Trump dangled the Patriot-production license as an answer to Kyiv’s long-term air-defense needs.

When Zelensky and Stefanishyna met again with Trump last week, ahead of Graham’s funeral in Washington, the tensions of the previous year’s encounter were absent. Rather than arguing for support on moral and legal grounds, Zelensky touted Ukraine’s battlefield advantage and the expertise that Kyiv could offer in waging war in the 21st century. The message was that “Ukraine is no longer a charity case” but rather a valuable partner holding its own on the battlefield, a former Zelensky adviser told us after the meeting. “It was a much more realistic approach, given the administration’s ‘America First’ policy. And if you look at the results, it’s night and day.” Now it was Putin, not Zelensky, whom U.S. officials viewed as the obstacle to peace. Even Laura Loomer, an informal Trump adviser and erstwhile supporter of the Kremlin, returned from Kyiv gushing about how Ukraine deserved American backing to figure out how to win.

That was last week, shortly before we visited the Ukrainian embassy, which occupies a historic brick structure in Georgetown, north of the Potomac River. In 1791, President George Washington met with a group of local landholders in the building to discuss acquiring terrain for the American capital. Today, a hallway in the building holds a Ukrainian bomber drone called a Vampire, which Stefanishyna used to showcase her country’s wartime innovations.

On the day of our interview, however, Stefanishyna was preparing to leave after less than a year on the job. Investigative journalists in Kyiv had scrutinized her property deals and her record in government going back to 2013, when she served as a junior official in the justice ministry. The price her family had paid for an apartment in Kyiv nearly a decade later also raised suspicion in the press. Anti-corruption investigators began looking into her financial records, questioning her friends and relatives. She denied all of the claims of wrongdoing but decided that the allegations were too distracting for her to remain the ambassador to the U.S. “I cannot really pretend like I’m doing a great job here, having fun, while my family is under threat,” she said, tears welling in her eyes.

A week after we spoke with Stefanishyna, anti-corruption authorities in Kyiv charged her with “illicit enrichment,” and a court set her bail at 6 million hryvnia, worth roughly $130,000. “The mission has been successfully completed, and I am in Ukraine to answer here,” she wrote in response on social media. “The burden of proof lies with the one making the accusation. As for me, I will do all I can: calmly defend my position in accordance with the law.”

Her departure was part of a government reshuffle that also cost Fedorov, the defense minister, his job. Speaking last week to Ukrainian journalists, he said that his firing was also related to problems with corruption. In his role as the defense minister, he had pushed for reforms that angered a long list of arms manufacturers and their allies in the military high command, and they had teamed up to undermine Fedorov’s position. His allies told us that he has continued to try to persuade Musk to relent on Starlink, but to no avail.

In a matter of days, the optimism that for months had been building around Ukraine’s prospects seemed to fade. At one point earlier this summer, Zelensky could look ahead to an influx of new U.S. missiles to defend Kyiv, the right to make even more in Ukraine, and the potential ability to strike inside Russia thanks to Fedorov’s overtures to Musk. He enjoyed greater respect from Trump for Ukraine’s innovations and battlefield momentum, and better relations across Washington thanks to a well-regarded young ambassador.

Instead, Trump appears to have turned lukewarm and is stalling on previous commitments on Patriot missiles. Entreaties to Musk have so far failed. Zelensky’s firing of his popular defense minister has prompted protests at home. And Ukraine has no ambassador to make the case for continued U.S. support, because the previous one returned home to face charges of corruption.

As if to emphasize the turnaround, Russia has intensified its missile strikes on Kyiv, taking advantage of Ukraine’s depleted air defenses. Earlier this week, the city and its suburbs faced a barrage of at least two dozen ballistic missiles in a single night. Ukraine was unable to shoot any of them down. Seventeen civilians died, and at least 44 others were wounded.

entries.title: Trump Is Asking the Private Sector to Save Him
entries.summary: Piecemeal price cuts won’t solve the Iran war’s effects on inflation.
entries.content:
Piecemeal price cuts won’t solve the Iran war’s effects on inflation.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

At this year’s annual meeting of the World Economic Forum, Donald Trump told a room full of the world’s most prominent CEOs about a routine that he performs when he meets a successful businessperson:

I say, “Congratulations!”

They say, “On what?”

I said, “You’ve doubled your net worth since I’ve been president, right?”

This is how Trump has long pitched himself—as the savior of American commerce. One of his central promises to voters in 2024 was that he would encourage private investment in the United States, boosting the stock market and ushering in a “golden age” of economic activity. Everyone, he vowed, would be making money.

But the president now seems less pro-business than he once did. On Monday, in response to a question about the gargantuan profits being posted by U.S. oil companies, Trump told reporters that ExxonMobil and Chevron are “making too much money based on a shortage.” Energy companies adjust their prices as global markets move; when Trump took the country to war against Iran, in February, the world’s oil supply was abruptly pinched, and prices shot up. Chevron and ExxonMobil announced that they’d earned $12.1 billion and $14.5 billion, respectively, last quarter—many billions more than they’d made during the same period last year. “They ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price,” Trump said.

This statement echoes the president’s previous accusation of price gouging in the industry. Back in June, after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding, Trump claimed that companies were keeping gas prices from falling as quickly as oil prices were. There are legitimate economic reasons that gas prices and oil prices aren’t always perfectly synced, and Big Oil doesn’t unilaterally set retail gas prices at American pumps (fewer than 5 percent of U.S. gas stations are owned directly by major oil companies, according to the American Petroleum Institute). The Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission subsequently called for states to investigate possible retail-price manipulation. To shift some of the responsibility for high gas prices, the president is now scolding an industry he once championed—but it won’t change the reality that most Americans are unhappy with the economy, and that Trump is largely to blame.

Oil interests reportedly spent more than $75 million to get Trump reelected, and the administration has consistently supported the industry over the past two years. “Drill, baby, drill” has been a mantra for his administration since day one. The White House recently revoked protections for endangered species, clearing the way for companies to drill in critical wildlife habitats. The secretary of the interior, Doug Burgum, has pushed to increase offshore drilling and drilling on public lands. Trump’s suggestion that Big Oil return some of its money “to the public” represents, by his own admission, a hard pivot. “I should be the last one to say it, because I’m a big free-enterprise guy—nobody bigger,” he said on Monday. (ExxonMobil declined to comment for this story, Chevron didn’t respond to my request, and the White House told me that “President Trump’s priority has always been and continues to be lowering gas prices for American families.”)

The Trump administration has made a point of celebrating businesses that have cut costs for consumers in recent months. In July, Trump applauded a new chain of gas stations called the Freedom Fuel Network for selling gas at a discount across the mid-Atlantic. On Truth Social, the president wrote that this “VERY smart Retailer” was “stepping up” on account of its patriotism, and that others should follow its example. Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, wrote on X yesterday that a co-owner of 14 Piggly Wiggly supermarkets (who has been invited to the Oval Office in the past) was “answering Trump’s call” by “boldly stepping up to lower costs for families.” She praised Walmart for implementing similar price-cutting measures, and wrote a few days ago that another grocer, Meijer, was also “answering the call” by lowering prices on more than 1,000 items. But it’s unclear whether these companies’ discounts were actually responses to the president, as Rollins has suggested.

Trump and his party have every reason to be worried about high prices. All kinds of consumer goods have become more expensive since the start of the Iran war, and Americans are now broadly worried about the cost of living, just as they were before Trump took office. People’s dissatisfaction with the president’s handling of the economy is reflected in his abysmal approval ratings, which pose a problem for Republicans in the midterms. Trump’s strategy has so far been to avoid taking responsibility for any Iran-driven inflation and to insist that, actually, the U.S. is experiencing an economic boom. He’s right that some indicators have lately been positive: The stock market continues to set record highs, and inflation did cool in June after three straight months of acceleration—although it’s still higher than it was before the start of the war.

With his comments on Big Oil, the president seems to be acknowledging that high prices are indeed a problem for many Americans. He also seems to expect that private companies will bail him out during a moment of political weakness. This administration has created the conditions—both domestically and abroad—for consumer goods to become more expensive, and for the cost of oil to jump. No piecemeal discount can undo what Trump himself has already done.

Separating facts from lies, and real thoughts from fabrications, can seem more difficult than ever: Words and images are easily faked, and some writers at every stage—students, academics, novelists—are letting machines do the work for them. The author may as well be dead. Ubiquitous cameras are eroding human privacy, creating the sense that we live in a panopticon. And across many popular platforms, information is often shorn of context, if not outright false.

The fact that I feed my kids and pay my rent as a novelist and teacher likely intensifies the queasiness I feel at these developments. Yet my profession also helps me understand that the idea of society coming apart might be the oldest story in the world.
